benefits: Covers the six most-used 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and square pyramid.
Full-precision results with no rounding surprises.
Bonus surface-area and base-area rows computed automatically.
Works with any unit: mm, cm, m, in or ft.
Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

faqs.a: Volume measures the space inside a 3D shape, in cubic units (cm³, m³...). Surface area measures the outer skin, in square units. You need volume for capacity (how much fits inside) and surface area for material (paint, wrapping).
faqs.q: What is the difference between volume and surface area?

faqs.a: A cone fills exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height. This was known to the ancient Greeks — Democritus stated it and Eudoxus proved it. The pyramid is likewise one third of its box.
faqs.q: Why is a cone one third of a cylinder?

faqs.a: Yes — the unit selector changes only the label on the result. It does not convert between units, so enter all dimensions in the same unit you select.
faqs.q: Can I use inches or feet instead of cm?

faqs.a: The sphere formula comes from calculus: V = ∫π(r²−x²)dx from −r to r, which evaluates to (4/3)πr³. Archimedes found it geometrically and was so proud it was carved on his tomb.
faqs.q: Where does the sphere formula (4/3)πr³ come from?

faqs.a: The pyramid here has a square base: V = (1/3) × base² × height. For other bases, multiply the base area by the height and divide by three — the one-third rule works for any pyramid.
faqs.q: Does the pyramid have to have a square base?

volume-calculator.formula:
Cube:     V = a³
Cuboid:   V = l × w × h
Sphere:   V = (4/3)πr³
Cylinder: V = πr²h
Cone:     V = (1/3)πr²h
Pyramid (square base): V = (1/3) × b² × h

Prism rule: V = (area of base) × height
Pyramid/cone rule: V = (area of base) × height / 3
howTo: Choose the 3D shape from the dropdown.
Enter its dimensions — every value in the same unit.
Pick the unit label (mm, cm, m, in, ft) for the result.
Read the volume, shown in cubic units.
Check the bonus row for surface area or base area where available.
keyFacts: Volume is always measured in cubic units (cm³, m³, in³...).
A sphere holds the most volume for the least surface of any shape.
Doubling every dimension multiplies the volume by eight (cube scaling).
Cones and pyramids hold exactly one third of their matching cylinder/box.
1 cm³ of water weighs 1 gram — which is how the metric system was designed.

limitations: Only the six listed shapes are supported — irregular shapes need numerical methods.
All dimensions must use the same unit; the tool does not convert between units.
Results assume perfect geometric shapes; real containers have wall thickness.
Display rounds to 8 significant digits; the underlying math uses full precision.

volume-calculator.quickAnswer: Pick a shape and enter its dimensions — for example a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm holds π × 9 × 5 = 141.372 cm³. Cube, cuboid, sphere, cone and square pyramid are supported, in mm, cm, m, in or ft.
volume-calculator.tagline: Volumes of cubes, cuboids, spheres, cylinders, cones and pyramids.
volume-calculator.workedExample:
Cylinder with r = 3 cm, h = 5 cm:
V = πr²h = π × 3² × 5 = π × 9 × 5 = 45π ≈ 141.372 cm³

Sphere with r = 3 cm:
V = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × π × 27 = 36π ≈ 113.097 cm³

Cone with r = 3 cm, h = 5 cm:
V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × π × 9 × 5 = 15π ≈ 47.124 cm³ — exactly one third of the matching cylinder.
